subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: State the meaning of 'Not-for-Profit' Organisations.
answer_text: Not-for-Profit Organisations (NPO) are set up with the prime objective of providing services and not to earn profit thereby enhancing the welfare of society. Such organisations include schools, hospitals, trade unions, religious organisations, etc. The person/s or the groups of individuals who govern and manage the working of an NPO are known as trustees. NPO's main sources of income are donations, subscriptions, life membership fees, grants etc. As these organisations are not set up with profit motive, they do not prepare Trading and Profit and Loss Account. Instead, they maintain Receipt and Payments Account, Income and Expenditure Account and Balance Sheet.
final_answer: Thus, NPOs focus on service rather than profit.
difficulty_reasoning: Direct recall of the definition of NPOs.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: State the meaning of Receipt and Payment Account.
answer_text: Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of the Cash Book. All cash receipts are recorded on the Receipts side (i.e. Debit side) and all cash payments are recorded on the Payments side (i.e. Credit side) of Receipts and Payments Account. It is prepared on the basis of cash and bank transactions recorded in the Cash Book. It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank and ends with the closing balances of cash and bank (balancing figure) at the end of the accounting period. It records all cash and bank transactions both of capital and revenue nature. It not only records the cash and bank transactions relating to the current accounting period, but also the cash and bank receipts (or payments) received during the current accounting period that may be related to the previous or next accounting period.
final_answer: Therefore, it helps in assessing the cash position of an NPO.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of cash book summarization.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: State the meaning of Income and Expenditure Account.
answer_text: Income and Expenditure Account (I&E) is similar to the Profit and Loss Account in the sense that while the former is prepared to ascertain surplus or deficit during an accounting period, the latter is prepared to ascertain net profit or net loss incurred during an accounting period. I&E Account is a nominal account and is prepared on the accrual basis. It records all transactions of revenue nature that are related to the current accounting period (whether outstanding or prepaid) for which the books are maintained. All expenses and losses are recorded on the debit side (Expenditure side) and all income and gains are recorded on the credit side (Income side) of I&E Account. The closing balance or the balancing figure of I&E Account is termed as surplus (or deficit), if the sum total of the Income side exceeds (is lesser than) the sum total of the Expenditure side.
final_answer: Thus, it helps in determining the financial performance of an NPO.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of accounting principles.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: What are the features of Receipt and Payment Account?
answer_text:
The following are the features of Receipt and Payment Account:
1. Nature: It is a Real Account. It is a summarised version of Cash Book.
2. Nature of Transactions: It records only cash and bank transactions. Transactions other than cash and bank like depreciation, loss/ profit on sale of assets, etc. are not recorded in this account.
3. No distinction between Capital and Revenue items: It records all cash and bank receipts and payments of both capital and revenue nature.
4. Opening and closing balance: It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank and ends with the closing balance of the cash and bank (balancing figure) at the end of the accounting period.
5. Purpose: It reveals the cash position of an organisation. It helps to ascertain the total amount paid and received during an accounting period.
final_answer: Thus, it provides a clear view of cash transactions.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of the features of accounting accounts.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: What steps are taken to prepare Income and Expenditure Account from a Receipt and Payment Account?

parts.part_text: Step 1: All the revenue expenditures paid for the current accounting period are transferred from the Payments side of R&P to the Expenditure side of I&E.
Step 2: All the revenue receipts for the current accounting period are transferred from the Receipts side of R&P to the Income side of I&E.

Step 3: Expenses outstanding for the current period and expenses paid in advance (prepaid expenses) for the current period in the preceding accounting periods are to be added (adjusted) to their related expenses in the Step 1.

Step 4: Income outstanding (accrued income) for the current period and income received in advance for the current period in the preceding accounting periods are to be added (adjusted) to their related incomes in Step 2.
Step 5: Non-cash items like depreciation, appreciation for the current accounting period are to be adjusted in the I&E.

Step 6: After adjusting all the revenue items for the current accounting period, the Income and the Expenditure sides are totaled. If the sum total of the Income side exceeds (or is lesser than) the sum total of the Expenditure side, then the balancing figure is termed as surplus (or deficit).

difficulty_reasoning: Involves multiple steps and understanding of accounting processes.

question_text: What is subscription? How is it calculated?
answer_text: Subscription is the main source of income for an NPO besides entrance fees, donations, grants, etc. Subscriptions refer to the amount of money paid by the members on periodic basis for keeping their membership with the organisation alive. It is paid monthly, quarterly, half yearly or annually by the members. It is shown in the debit side of the Receipt and Payment Account with the total amount received during the year that may be related to the current period and to the previous and next accounting period.
final_answer: Thus, it is crucial for maintaining the financial health of an NPO.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of subscription and its role in NPOs.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: What is Capital Fund? How is it calculated?
answer_text: Capital fund is the excess of NPOs' assets over its liabilities. In other words, the excess of assets over the liabilities for a profit earning organisation is termed as capital and the same for an NPO is termed as capital fund. Any surplus or deficit ascertained from Income and Expenditure account is added to (deducted from) the capital fund. It is also termed as Accumulated Fund.
final_answer: Thus, it represents the net worth of an NPO.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of capital fund and its calculation.

question_text: Explain the statement: “Receipt and Payment Account is a summarised version of Cash Book”.
answer_text: Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of the Cash Book. This account is prepared by those organisations which maintain their books on cash basis. All cash receipts are recorded on the Receipts side (i.e. Debit side) and all cash payments are recorded on the Payments side (i.e. Credit side) of Receipts and Payments Account. It is prepared on the basis of cash and bank transactions recorded in the Cash Book. It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank and ends with the closing balances of cash and bank (balancing figure) at the end of the accounting period. It records all the cash and bank transactions both of capital and revenue nature. It not only records the cash and bank transactions relating to the current accounting period, but also cash and bank receipts (or payments) received during the current accounting period that may be related to the previous or next accounting period. This account only helps us to ascertain the closing balance of the cash and bank and helps in assessing the cash position of an NPO. It also forms the basis for the preparation of Income and Expenditure Account.
final_answer: Thus, on the basis of the above mentioned points and similarities, the statement 'Receipt and Payment Account is a summarised version of Cash Book' is justified.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of accounting concepts and summarization.

question_text: “Income and Expenditure Account of a Not-for-Profit Organisation is akin to Profit and Loss Account of a business concern”. Explain the statement.
answer_text: Income and Expenditure Account (I&E) is similar to Profit and Loss Account (P&L), in the sense that the former is prepared by Not-for-profit-Organisations and the latter is prepared by profit earning organisations. Both the accounts are prepared on the accrual basis. Similar to the P&L, all the expenses and losses pertaining to the current accounting period are recorded on the debit side (Expenditure side) and all the gains and income of the current accounting period are recorded on the credit side (Income side) of the I&E. The balancing figure of the I&E is surplus or deficit and that of the P&L is net profit or net loss. Both the accounts record only revenue items which are related to the current accounting period.
final_answer: Thus, both the accounts are prepared on the accrual basis.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of accounting principles and comparison.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: Distinguish between Receipts and Payments Account and Income and Expenditure Account.
answer_text:
1. Nature: Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of cash and bank transactions, while Income and Expenditure Account is a summary of current year transactions.
2. Revenue and Capital: Receipts and Payments Account records transactions related to both revenue and capital nature, whereas Income and Expenditure Account records transactions related to revenue nature only.
3. Debit Side: The debit side of Receipts and Payments Account records cash and bank receipts during an accounting period, while the debit side of Income and Expenditure Account records expenses incurred in the current accounting period.
4. Credit Side: The credit side of Receipts and Payments Account records payments in cash and through cheques, while the credit side of Income and Expenditure Account records income earned in the current accounting period.
5. Type of Account: Receipts and Payments Account is a Real Account, while Income and Expenditure Account is a Nominal Account.
6. Period: Receipts and Payments Account records receipts and payments made during the year that may be related to the current accounting period or the preceding period and the succeeding accounting period, while Income and Expenditure Account only records income and expenditure for the current accounting period.
7. Object: Receipts and Payments Account depicts the cash position of an NPO, while Income and Expenditure Account shows the net result or deficits due to the business activities during the year.
8. Opening Balance: Receipts and Payments Account begins with the opening balance of cash in hand and cash at bank or overdraft, while Income and Expenditure Account usually has no opening balance.
9. Closing Balance: The balancing figure of Receipts and Payments Account is expressed in terms of the closing balance of cash in hand and cash at bank or overdraft, while the balancing figure of Income and Expenditure Account is expressed as surplus (if incomes > expenses) or deficits (if expenses > incomes).
10. Depreciation: Receipts and Payments Account does not include non-cash items like depreciation, while Income and Expenditure Account includes non-cash items like bad debts, provisions, etc. in order to determine net profit or net loss.
11. Adjustment: Receipts and Payments during the year can be adjusted before preparation of the financial statements, while adjustments regarding both capital and revenue transactions can be made in Income and Expenditure Account.
final_answer: Thus, both accounts serve different purposes and have distinct characteristics.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires detailed understanding and comparison of two accounting concepts.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: Explain the basic features of Income and Expenditure Account and of Receipt and Payment Account.
answer_text: Income and Expenditure Account (I&E) is a Nominal Account and is prepared on the accrual basis. It records all transactions of revenue nature that are related to the current accounting period (whether outstanding or prepaid) for which the books are maintained. All expenses and losses are recorded on the debit side (Expenditure side) and all income and gains are recorded on the credit side (Income side) of I&E Account. The closing balance or the balancing figure of I&E Account is termed as surplus (or deficit), if the sum total of the Income side exceeds (is lesser than) the sum total of the Expenditure side. The following are the basic features of Income and Expenditure Account: 1. Nature: It is a Nominal Account. The debit side of I&E records all expenses and losses and the credit side records all incomes and gains related to the current accounting period. 2. Basis: It is prepared on the basis of Receipt and Payment Account (R&P). All the revenues items whether incomes or expenditures are transferred from R&P. 3. Excludes Capital Transactions: The transactions those are capital in nature are excluded from this account. For example, only profit or loss on sale of fixed assets is recorded but the total amount of sales is not recorded since sale of fixed asset is considered as a capital receipt. 4. Akin to Profit and Loss Account: Income and Expenditure Account (I&E) is similar to the Profit and Loss Account in the sense that while the former is prepared to ascertain surplus or deficit during an accounting period the latter is prepared to ascertain net profit or net loss incurred during an accounting period. 5. Records only Current Year's items: This account records only those transactions that are related to current accounting year. In other words, transactions related to the preceding or succeeding accounting period are excluded even if these transactions are realised in the current period. 6. Adjustments: Various cash and non-cash items like, outstanding expenses, prepaid expenses, income received in advance, income due but not received, depreciation, bad debts, etc. can be adjusted in this account. 7. Balancing Figure: The balancing figure of this account is expressed in terms of either surplus (if incomes > expenses) or deficit (if expenses > incomes). The surplus balance, if any, is added to the Capital Fund, whereas, the deficit balance, if any, is deducted from the Capital Fund. Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of the Cash Book. All the cash receipts are recorded on the Receipts side (i.e. Debit side) and all the cash payments are recorded on the Payments side (i.e. Credit side) of Receipts and Payments Account. It is prepared on the basis of cash and bank transactions recorded in the Cash Book. It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank and ends with the closing balances of cash and bank (balancing figure) at the end of the accounting period. It records all the cash and bank transactions both of capital and revenue nature. It not only records the cash and bank transactions relating to the current accounting period but also cash and bank receipts (or payments) received during the current accounting period that may be related to the previous or next accounting period. The following are the features of Receipt and Payment Account: 1. Nature: It is a Real Account. It is a summarised version of the Cash Book.
final_answer: The Income and Expenditure Account and Receipt and Payment Account serve distinct purposes in accounting for not-for-profit organizations, with specific features that define their operation.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of accounting principles and the ability to explain features.

question_text: Show the treatment of the following items by a Not-for-Profit Organisation: (i) Annual subscription (ii) Specific donation (iii) Sale of fixed assets (iv) Sale of old periodicals (v) Sale of sports materials (vi) Life membership fee.

parts.part_text: Annual Subscription
parts.answer_text: a) Subscriptions received during an accounting year (whether related to the current year or previous and subsequent year) are shown on the debit side of the Receipts and Payments Account. b) Subscription amount related to the current accounting year only, whether received or yet to be received are shown on the credit side of the Income and Expenditure Account. c) Subscriptions received in advance for the subsequent year are shown on the Liabilities side of the Balance Sheet. d) Subscriptions due but not received are shown in the Assets side of the Balance Sheet.
parts.final_answer: Thus, the treatment of annual subscriptions involves recording them in both the Receipts and Payments Account and the Income and Expenditure Account, depending on their timing and nature.

parts.part_text: Specific donation
parts.answer_text: a) The amount received for specific donation is shown on the debit side of the Receipts and Payments Accounts. b) The amount received for specific donation is shown on the Liabilities side of the Balance Sheet as it is used for the specific purpose for which it is received.
parts.final_answer: Specific donations are recorded in the Receipts and Payments Account and shown as liabilities in the Balance Sheet.

parts.part_text: Sale of fixed assets
parts.answer_text: a) The amount received from the sale of fixed assets are recorded on the debit side of the Receipts and Payments Account. b) Profit (or loss) on the sale of fixed assets is credited (or debited) to the Income and Expenditure Account. c) The book-value of the fixed assets sold is deducted from its respective assets on the Assets side of the Balance Sheet.
parts.final_answer: The sale of fixed assets is recorded in the Receipts and Payments Account, with profits or losses affecting the Income and Expenditure Account.

parts.part_text: Sale of old periodicals
parts.answer_text: a) The amount received from the sale of old periodicals are shown on the debit side of the Receipts and Payments Account. b) As the sale of old periodicals by any organisation is considered as revenue receipts, so it is shown on the credit side of the Income and Expenditure Account.
parts.final_answer: Sales of old periodicals are recorded in both accounts, reflecting their nature as revenue receipts.

parts.part_text: Sale of sports materials
parts.answer_text: a) The amount received from the sale of sport materials are debited to the Receipt and Payments Account. b) As the sale of sport materials by any sport club is considered as revenue income, so it is shown on the credit side of the Income and Expenditure Account.
parts.final_answer: The sale of sports materials is treated similarly to other revenue items, recorded in both accounts.

parts.part_text: Life membership fee
parts.answer_text: a) The amount paid by a person to become a member of an organisation is called life membership fees. As this is a receipt for an NPO, so it is debited to the Receipt and Payment Account. b) Life Membership fees is not recurring in nature and received once for a whole life from a member. Thus, as Life Membership Fees are capital receipts, so these are added to the Capital Fund on the Liabilities side of the Balance Sheet.
parts.final_answer: Life membership fees are recorded in the Receipts and Payments Account and treated as capital receipts in the Balance Sheet.

final_answer: The treatment of various items by a Not-for-Profit Organisation involves specific accounting practices for each type of receipt.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of accounting treatments for various transactions.

question_text: What is Receipt and Payment Account? How is it different from Income and Expenditure Account?
answer_text: Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of the Cash Book. All the cash receipts are recorded on the Receipts side (i.e. Debit side) and all the cash payments are recorded on the Payments side (i.e. Credit side) of Receipts and Payments Account. It is prepared on the basis of cash and bank transactions recorded in the Cash Book. It begins with the opening balance of cash and bank and ends with the closing balances of cash and bank (balancing figure) at the end of the accounting period. It records all cash and bank transactions both of capital and revenue nature. It not only records cash and bank transactions relating to the current accounting period, but also cash and bank receipts (or payments) received during the current accounting period that may be related to the previous or next accounting period.
final_answer: Thus, the Receipts and Payments Account summarizes cash transactions, while the Income and Expenditure Account summarizes income and expenses for the period.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires understanding of accounting concepts and differentiation between two types of accounts.

subject: accountancy_2
chapter_name: accounting for not for profit organisation
question_text: Distinguish between Receipts and Payments Account and Income and Expenditure Account.
answer_text:
1. Nature: Receipts and Payments Account is a summary of cash and bank transactions; Income and Expenditure Account is a summary of current year income and expenses.
2. Revenue and Capital: Receipts and Payments Account records transactions related to both revenue and capital nature; Income and Expenditure Account records transactions related to revenue nature only.
3. Debit Side: Debit side of Receipts and Payments Account records cash and bank receipts; Debit side of Income and Expenditure Account records expenses and losses incurred.
4. Credit Side: Credit side of Receipts and Payments Account records payments; Credit side of Income and Expenditure Account records income and gains earned.
5. Type of Account: Receipts and Payments Account is a Real Account; Income and Expenditure Account is a Nominal Account.
6. Period: Receipts and Payments Account records receipts and payments made during the year; Income and Expenditure Account records income and expenditure made during the current accounting period.
7. Object: Receipts and Payments Account depicts the cash position of an NPO; Income and Expenditure Account shows the net result in terms of surplus or deficits due to business activities during the year.
8. Opening Balance: Receipts and Payments Account begins with the opening balance of cash; Income and Expenditure Account usually has no opening balance.
9. Closing Balance: Closing balance of Receipts and Payments Account is expressed in terms of cash; Closing balance of Income and Expenditure Account is expressed in terms of surplus or deficit.
10. Depreciation: Receipts and Payments Account does not include non-cash items; Income and Expenditure Account includes non-cash items like depreciation.
11. Adjustment: Adjustments can be made in Receipts and Payments Account; Adjustments regarding both cash and non-cash transactions can be made in Income and Expenditure Account.
12. Transfer of Balance: Opening balance of Receipts and Payments Account is carried forward; Closing balance of Income and Expenditure Account is added or deducted from the Capital Fund.
13. System: Receipts and Payments Account is prepared on a cash basis; Income and Expenditure Account is prepared on an accrual basis.
final_answer: In summary, the two accounts serve different purposes and are prepared using different accounting principles.
difficulty_reasoning: Requires detailed understanding and comparison of two accounting concepts.
